articles.title: Type 2 diabetes breakthrough as 54% achieve remission in just 6 months
articles.summary: A promising new study suggests that more than half of younger adults with type 2 diabetes could achieve remission in just six months through a combination of a low-calorie diet and structured exercise. Researchers found that 54% of participants under age 45 who followed an intensive diet and exercise program achieved remission, compared with just 4% receiving usual care.
articles.content:
A carefully structured combination of diet and exercise may offer a powerful way to put type 2 diabetes into remission in younger adults. In a new clinical trial, more than half of participants who followed an intensive lifestyle program achieved remission within just six months, compared with only 4% of those receiving standard care.

The findings, presented at the Annual Meeting of the European Association for the Study of Diabetes (EASD) and published in The Lancet Regional Health Americas, suggest that a low-calorie diet paired with regular exercise could significantly change the course of early-onset type 2 diabetes (EOT2D) (aged under 45 years).

The research was conducted by Professor Kaberi Dasgupta, Director of the Division of General Internal Medicine at McGill University in Montreal, Canada, Professor Thomas Yates of the University of Leicester in the UK, and their colleagues.

Why Early-Onset Type 2 Diabetes Is Especially Dangerous

Type 2 diabetes diagnosed at a younger age can be particularly aggressive. People with early-onset type 2 diabetes (EOT2D) often experience a faster decline in blood sugar control, develop complications earlier in life, and face a shorter life expectancy than those diagnosed at older ages.

Previous research has shown that very low-calorie diets (LEDs) can lower blood sugar enough for some people to achieve remission without diabetes medication (T2D remission). Remission means blood sugar has fallen below the threshold used to diagnose diabetes and remains there without glucose-lowering drugs. However, it does not necessarily mean the disease has been permanently cured.

Researchers wanted to find out whether adding structured exercise could make this approach even more effective. Beyond helping regulate blood sugar, physical activity could improve fitness, protect muscle during weight loss, strengthen heart function, and reduce insulin resistance.

To investigate, the team tested whether combining a low-calorie diet with supervised exercise could achieve remission after 24 weeks, compared with standard medical care.

An Intensive Diet and Exercise Program

The randomized clinical trial took place at three research centers in England and Canada (affiliated with the University of Leicester, UK, McGill University (Montreal), and the University of Alberta, Edmonton). It enrolled adults aged 18 to 45 who had early-onset type 2 diabetes and obesity but were not using insulin.

The trial was open-label, meaning participants and researchers knew which treatment each person received, although the assessment of the main outcome was blinded.

One group continued receiving usual care. The other followed an intensive program that combined a daily intake of 800 to 900 calories with supervised aerobic and resistance exercise twice per week, plus one independent exercise session each week (weeks 1-12). Participants then transitioned to a diet designed to maintain their weight loss while continuing to exercise independently (weeks 13-24).

The researchers measured how many participants achieved diabetes remission after 24 weeks. To qualify, participants needed an HbA1c level below 6.5%, equivalent to 48 mmol/mol, and must have taken no glucose-lowering medication for at least 12 weeks. HbA1c is a blood test that reflects average blood sugar levels over approximately three months.

The analysis included everyone assigned to either group. When remission data were missing, researchers conservatively counted those participants as not having achieved remission. They also examined changes in cardiovascular fitness, body composition, and heart structure.

What Participants Ate During the Study

At the beginning of the intensive program, participants discontinued medications used to lower blood sugar and blood pressure (in the absence of albuminuria), under the study's medical supervision. Albuminuria refers to the presence of a protein called albumin in urine and can indicate kidney damage.

Their restricted diet provided 800 to 900 calories daily (30% protein, 50% carbohydrate, 20% fat). Participants were encouraged to drink at least two liters of calorie-free fluids each day and were given access to a fiber-based laxative when needed.

During the first two weeks, all meals were replaced with specially formulated nutritional products (Optifast). From weeks three through 12, participants maintained the same calorie limit but gained more flexibility in their food choices (Optifast in UK and ProtiDiet in Canada).

This second phase allowed one conventional meal per day, with daily intake targets that included protein, fruit, and vegetables (60 to 90 g protein from all sources combined, one portion of fruit, two portions of non-starchy vegetables).

After the first 12 weeks, participants shifted toward maintaining their weight loss rather than continuing rapid weight reduction.

More Than Half Achieved Type 2 Diabetes Remission

Between September 24, 2021, and June 6, 2025, the researchers enrolled and randomly assigned 96 participants (40 UK, 56 Canada). The group included 50 people assigned to the intensive intervention and 46 receiving standard care (24 female, 26 male intervention group; 21 female, 25 male control group; mean age 38 years, BMI 35·2 kg/m2).

Of those enrolled, 86 (90%) completed the final assessments.

The results revealed a striking difference between the groups. After 24 weeks, 27 of the 50 participants following the diet and exercise program had achieved remission, representing 54% of the intervention group. In comparison, just two of the 46 participants receiving standard care reached remission, or approximately 4%.

After accounting for relevant statistical factors, the researchers calculated that participants in the intensive lifestyle program were 21 times more likely to achieve remission than those receiving usual care.

Weight loss was also substantially greater among participants following the combined program.

Among the 47 intervention participants with available weight data, average body weight fell from 100.7 kg to 92.3 kg, a reduction of 8.4 kg over 24 weeks. The 43 control participants with available weight data started at an average of 103.2 kg and lost just 1.2 kg, reaching 102.0 kg.

After statistical adjustment, the intervention group lost an average of 7.5 kg more weight than the control group. Importantly, this included an additional 6.6 kg of fat loss, indicating that much of the difference came from reduced body fat.

Promising Results With Manageable Side Effects

No severe adverse events were reported during the trial. However, side effects were more common among participants following the intensive diet.

At least one adverse event occurred in 43 of the 50 intervention participants, compared with six of the 46 participants receiving standard care. Most problems appeared during the early stages of the restrictive diet and included symptoms such as constipation, headaches, dizziness, and fatigue (e.g., constipation, headache, dizziness, fatigue). These effects generally resolved.

The researchers believe the findings demonstrate that a combined diet and exercise intervention can produce meaningful improvements beyond blood sugar control alone.

The authors say: "Our findings demonstrate the feasibility and efficacy of combining structured aerobic and resistance exercise with a low energy diet in early-onset type 2 diabetes, supporting its potential to deliver substantial and holistic health and well-being benefits alongside diabetes remission.

"Our remission rates are at the upper end of those previously reported in the literature for trials of similar duration, reinforcing the potential of structured lifestyle interventions to support clinically meaningful remission, while demonstrating for the first time that such effects can be achieved in a multi-ethnic population with early-onset type 2 diabetes through a combined low-energy diet and structured exercise intervention."

Why Preserving Muscle During Weight Loss Matters

One particularly important aspect of the study was its emphasis on protecting muscle mass during rapid weight loss.

The researchers explain that most people who complete weight loss programs eventually regain some or all of the weight they lost. This is especially relevant when using very low-calorie diets to achieve diabetes remission.

Losing weight through calorie restriction alone typically reduces both fat and fat-free mass, which includes muscle. Some evidence suggests that when weight returns, the body may regain proportionally more fat than lean tissue.

Over time, repeated weight loss and regain could therefore contribute to a gradual reduction in muscle mass and increase the risk of sarcopenia, a condition characterized by declining muscle mass and strength.

To address this problem, the researchers incorporated resistance training into the most intensive phase of weight loss. Their results suggest that it is possible to achieve substantial fat loss while preserving muscle, potentially making the approach more beneficial for long-term metabolic health.

They say: "Our RESET for Remission study targeted muscle during the intensive weight loss phase through resistance training, and our findings indicate fat-free mass and muscle preservation is achievable with rapid weight loss. Preserving muscle during remission-oriented weight loss may have important implications for long-term metabolic health, physical function, and disease trajectory. This requires examination in a longer-term study."

A Potential New Approach to Treating Type 2 Diabetes

The findings could be particularly important as type 2 diabetes becomes increasingly common among younger adults worldwide.

People who develop the condition earlier in life face more years of exposure to elevated blood sugar, increasing their lifetime risk of cardiovascular disease and other complications. Finding effective ways to achieve remission early could therefore have substantial health benefits.

The researchers emphasize that their intervention did more than lower blood sugar. It also reduced body fat while protecting muscle, improved muscle quality and physical performance, supported cardiovascular health, and produced improvements in participants' reported well-being.

They also suggest that this strategy could be especially relevant for people planning a pregnancy or who may become pregnant.

However, the researchers caution that longer studies are needed to determine whether the benefits can be sustained. In particular, future research must establish how well participants maintain their weight loss, muscle mass, and diabetes remission after returning to everyday life outside a closely monitored clinical trial.

The authors conclude: "By focusing specifically on early-onset type 2 diabetes, our trial addresses a growing clinical population, characterized by elevated cardiovascular disease risk, greater cumulative complication burden, and poor long-term outcomes…In summary, RESET for Remission demonstrated that in early-onset type 2 diabetes, combining structured aerobic and resistance exercise with a low-calorie diet produces high remission rates, induces fat loss while preserving muscle mass, improves muscle quality and function, enhances cardiovascular health, and leads to meaningful improvements in patient-reported outcomes. As the prevalence of early-onset type 2 diabetes rises globally, our findings highlight an opportunity to re-evaluate treatment paradigms and support scalable implementation of integrated dietary and exercise interventions for remission. Our approach may be particularly valuable in those seeking or with potential for pregnancy. It warrants further evaluation in longer term studies in real-world settings."
articles.reasoning: The article reports a significant clinical trial breakthrough showing that a combined low-calorie diet and structured exercise program can induce remission in over half of younger adults with early-onset type 2 diabetes within six months. This has broad public health implications given the rising prevalence of type 2 diabetes in younger populations and the aggressive nature of early-onset diabetes. The study is detailed, with clear methodology, measurable outcomes, and potential for large-scale impact on treatment paradigms and patient quality of life.
articles.personality_title: New diet and exercise program puts type 2 diabetes into remission for over half of young adults
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Type 2 diabetes is a disease where the body has trouble controlling blood sugar. When it starts at a young age, it can cause serious health problems faster than when diagnosed later in life. Finding ways to control or reverse this disease early is very important.

**What happened** – A study tested a new treatment for adults under 45 with early-onset type 2 diabetes. Ninety-six people joined the trial in the UK and Canada. Half followed a strict plan of eating only 800-900 calories a day and doing supervised exercise for six months. The other half received regular medical care. After 24 weeks, 54% of the people on the diet and exercise plan reached diabetes remission, meaning their blood sugar was normal without needing medication. Only 4% of the regular care group achieved this.

**Impact** – This result is important because it shows that combining a low-calorie diet with regular aerobic and muscle-strengthening exercise can greatly improve health in young adults with type 2 diabetes. The program also helped people lose fat while keeping muscle, which is good for long-term health. No serious side effects happened, and most minor issues like headaches went away quickly.

**What's next step** – Researchers want to study if these benefits last over a longer time and when people live their normal daily lives outside the study. They also want to see if this plan can help more people, including those preparing for pregnancy. If successful, this approach could change how doctors treat early type 2 diabetes worldwide.

**One-sentence takeaway** – A combined low-calorie diet and exercise program helped over half of young adults with early type 2 diabetes reach remission within six months, offering a promising new treatment option.
articles.personality_title_fr: Un nouveau programme de régime et d’exercice fait entrer le diabète de type 2 en rémission chez plus de la moitié des jeunes adultes
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Le diabète de type 2 est une maladie où le corps a du mal à contrôler le sucre dans le sang. Lorsqu’elle débute tôt, elle peut causer des problèmes de santé graves plus rapidement que lorsqu’elle est diagnostiquée plus tard. Trouver des moyens de contrôler ou inverser cette maladie tôt est très important.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Une étude a testé un nouveau traitement pour des adultes de moins de 45 ans atteints de diabète de type 2 précoce. Quatre-vingt-seize personnes ont participé à l’essai au Royaume-Uni et au Canada. La moitié a suivi un plan strict avec seulement 800 à 900 calories par jour et un exercice supervisé pendant six mois. L’autre moitié a reçu des soins médicaux habituels. Après 24 semaines, 54 % des personnes suivant le régime et l’exercice ont atteint la rémission du diabète, c’est-à-dire un taux de sucre normal sans médicament. Seulement 4 % du groupe de soins habituels y sont parvenus.

**Impact** – Ce résultat est important car il montre que combiner un régime hypocalorique avec un exercice régulier aérobie et de renforcement musculaire peut grandement améliorer la santé des jeunes adultes atteints de diabète de type 2. Le programme a aussi aidé à perdre de la graisse tout en conservant les muscles, ce qui est bon pour la santé à long terme. Aucun effet secondaire grave n’a été signalé, et les problèmes mineurs comme les maux de tête ont rapidement disparu.

**Prochaine étape** – Les chercheurs veulent étudier si ces bénéfices durent plus longtemps et lorsque les participants reprennent leur vie normale. Ils souhaitent aussi voir si ce plan peut aider plus de personnes, notamment celles qui préparent une grossesse. Si c’est concluant, cette méthode pourrait changer la façon dont les médecins traitent le diabète de type 2 précoce dans le monde.

**Une phrase clé** – Un programme combinant régime hypocalorique et exercice a permis à plus de la moitié des jeunes adultes atteints de diabète de type 2 précoce d’obtenir une rémission en six mois, offrant une nouvelle option de traitement prometteuse.
articles.personality_title_es: Nuevo programa de dieta y ejercicio logra remisión del diabetes tipo 2 en más de la mitad de adultos jóvenes
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – La diabetes tipo 2 es una enfermedad donde el cuerpo tiene dificultad para controlar el azúcar en la sangre. Cuando comienza a una edad joven, puede causar problemas de salud graves más rápido que si se diagnostica más tarde. Encontrar maneras de controlar o revertir esta enfermedad temprano es muy importante.

**Qué pasó** – Un estudio probó un nuevo tratamiento para adultos menores de 45 años con diabetes tipo 2 de inicio temprano. Noventa y seis personas participaron en el ensayo en Reino Unido y Canadá. La mitad siguió un plan estricto de comer solo 800 a 900 calorías al día y hacer ejercicio supervisado durante seis meses. La otra mitad recibió cuidado médico habitual. Después de 24 semanas, el 54 % de las personas en el plan de dieta y ejercicio lograron la remisión de la diabetes, es decir, niveles normales de azúcar sin necesitar medicamentos. Solo el 4 % del grupo de cuidado habitual logró esto.

**Impacto** – Este resultado es importante porque muestra que combinar una dieta baja en calorías con ejercicio aeróbico regular y entrenamiento de fuerza puede mejorar mucho la salud en adultos jóvenes con diabetes tipo 2. El programa también ayudó a perder grasa mientras se mantenía el músculo, algo bueno para la salud a largo plazo. No hubo efectos secundarios graves, y los problemas menores como dolores de cabeza desaparecieron rápido.

**Próximo paso** – Los investigadores quieren estudiar si estos beneficios duran más tiempo y cuando las personas vuelven a su vida normal fuera del estudio. También quieren ver si este plan puede ayudar a más personas, incluyendo quienes planean un embarazo. Si tiene éxito, este método podría cambiar cómo los médicos tratan la diabetes tipo 2 temprana en todo el mundo.

**Una frase clave** – Un programa combinado de dieta baja en calorías y ejercicio ayudó a más de la mitad de adultos jóvenes con diabetes tipo 2 temprana a lograr la remisión en seis meses, ofreciendo una nueva opción de tratamiento prometedora.

articles.title: Scientists confirm fruit and vegetable skin really is good for you
articles.summary: Parts of plants that are usually wasted, from kiwi skin to squash seeds, contain more fibre than the parts of the plant we do eat
articles.content:
Parts of plants that are usually wasted, from kiwi skin to squash seeds, contain more fibre than the parts of the plant we do eat

Fruit and vegetable skin is often rich in fibre Ekaterina Vasileva-Bagler/Getty Images

Some people are convinced that fruit and vegetable skin is particularly nutritious, and now scientists have confirmed the idea. They have discovered that these parts of fruits and vegetables often contain far more fibre than the flesh we normally consume.

The finding suggests cooks are unwittingly discarding fibre-rich food by chucking out the seeds, skins and stems of fruits and vegetables when preparing a meal.

Home cooks and caterers should adopt “root to tip” eating and start cooking with squash peel, watermelon rind and pepper stalks to improve the public’s intake of dietary fibre, the team says.

Advertisement

“We’ve really got to shift our purchasing habits to buy whole fruits and vegetables, and then use all of the fruits and vegetables in dishes,” says Rachel Gibson at King’s College London.

Gibson and her colleagues tested the fibre content of 12 fruits and vegetables, including butternut squash, kiwi fruit, watermelon, broccoli and bell pepper. The team measured the fibre content both in the parts typically consumed and the parts that usually go to waste.

They found that, in 10 of the 12 produce types, the normally wasted components contain more fibre than the commonly consumed parts. Butternut squash seeds and skin, for example, contained 9.25 grams of fibre per 100 grams, compared with 2 g of fibre per 100 g of squash flesh. Meanwhile, the skin and core of a pineapple core contains 450 per cent more fibre than the flesh. These skin and core components are often tough to chew, but the researchers say they can be blended, grated or roasted to make them more palatable.

Free newsletter Sign up to The Weekly Sign up to newsletter

Just 4 per cent of British adults meet the recommended minimum daily intake of 30 g of dietary fibre, with the average adult consuming around half that per day.

Gibson suggests caterers could use the findings to design fibre-rich meals using more produce that would otherwise go to waste. This could reduce food waste and cut costs for commercial kitchens, as well as increasing dietary fibre intake, she says.

King’s College London’s canteen piloted a “root to tip” menu in May 2025. Meals included a West African peanut stew made with all of a butternut squash, kale stalks and leek tops, and a watermelon salad featuring pickled watermelon rind.

Eating a larger proportion of harvested fruit and vegetables will also improve the resilience of the food system in the face of climate shocks, says Gibson. “Everything we pull out of the ground that we can eat, we should be eating.”

Christian Reynolds at City St George’s University of London says the research is an “exciting investigation”. But he points out that the most carbon-intensive food waste is meat and dairy products. Reducing fruit and vegetable waste is therefore “part of the solution, but it’s not the only thing we need to do”, he says.
articles.reasoning: The article reports a scientific discovery confirming that fruit and vegetable skins and other typically discarded parts contain significantly more dietary fibre than the commonly eaten portions. This finding encourages 'root to tip' eating, which can improve public health by increasing fibre intake, reduce food waste, and enhance food system resilience. The research has broad significance for the general public's nutrition and sustainable food practices, with detailed evidence and practical recommendations.
articles.personality_title: Scientists find fruit and vegetable skins have more fibre than the parts we eat
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Many people throw away parts of fruits and vegetables like skins, seeds, and stems when cooking. These parts are often seen as waste and not eaten.

**What happened** – Scientists from King’s College London tested 12 types of fruits and vegetables, including kiwi, squash, and watermelon. They found that in 10 out of 12, the skins, seeds, and cores had much more fibre than the parts we usually eat. For example, butternut squash seeds and skin have over four times more fibre than the squash flesh.

**Impact** – This discovery shows that by eating the whole fruit or vegetable, we can get more fibre, which is important for health. It also means less food is wasted, which can save money and help the environment. Since only 4% of adults in Britain eat enough fibre, using these parts could improve diets.

**What's next step** – Cooks and food services are encouraged to use all parts of fruits and vegetables when preparing meals. King’s College London tried this with a special menu using whole vegetables, like a stew with all parts of squash and a salad with watermelon rind. This way of cooking could become more common to reduce waste and boost fibre intake.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Eating fruit and vegetable skins and seeds can provide much more fibre and help reduce food waste and improve health.
articles.personality_title_fr: Les scientifiques confirment que la peau des fruits et légumes contient plus de fibres que la chair
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Beaucoup de gens jettent la peau, les graines et les tiges des fruits et légumes en cuisinant, pensant que ce sont des déchets.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Des scientifiques du King’s College de Londres ont analysé 12 fruits et légumes, comme le kiwi, la courge et la pastèque. Ils ont découvert que dans 10 cas sur 12, la peau, les graines et le cœur contiennent beaucoup plus de fibres que la partie que nous mangeons habituellement. Par exemple, les graines et la peau de la courge butternut ont plus de quatre fois plus de fibres que la chair.

**Impact** – Cette découverte montre qu’en mangeant tout le fruit ou légume, on peut avoir plus de fibres, importantes pour la santé. Cela réduit aussi le gaspillage alimentaire, ce qui permet d’économiser de l’argent et protège l’environnement. Seulement 4 % des adultes britanniques consomment assez de fibres, donc utiliser ces parties pourrait améliorer leur alimentation.

**Prochaine étape** – Les cuisiniers et les restaurateurs sont encouragés à utiliser toutes les parties des fruits et légumes dans leurs plats. Le King’s College a testé un menu spécial avec tous les morceaux, comme un ragoût avec toute la courge et une salade avec la peau de pastèque. Cette façon de cuisiner pourrait se généraliser pour réduire le gaspillage et augmenter la consommation de fibres.

**Résumé en une phrase** – Manger la peau et les graines des fruits et légumes apporte beaucoup plus de fibres, réduit le gaspillage et améliore la santé.
articles.personality_title_es: Científicos confirman que la piel de frutas y verduras tiene más fibra que la pulpa que comemos
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Muchas personas tiran la piel, semillas y tallos de frutas y verduras al cocinar, pensando que son desperdicios.

**Qué pasó** – Científicos del King’s College de Londres analizaron 12 frutas y verduras, como kiwi, calabaza y sandía. Descubrieron que en 10 de los 12 casos, la piel, semillas y el centro tienen mucha más fibra que la parte que normalmente comemos. Por ejemplo, las semillas y la piel de la calabaza butternut tienen más de cuatro veces la fibra que la pulpa.

**Impacto** – Este hallazgo muestra que al comer toda la fruta o verdura, obtenemos más fibra, que es importante para la salud. También reduce el desperdicio de comida, ahorrando dinero y ayudando al medio ambiente. Solo el 4 % de los adultos en el Reino Unido consume suficiente fibra, así que usar estas partes podría mejorar su dieta.

**Próximo paso** – Cocineros y servicios de comida están invitados a usar todas las partes de frutas y verduras en sus platos. El King’s College probó un menú especial usando todas las partes, como un guiso con toda la calabaza y una ensalada con la cáscara de sandía. Esta forma de cocinar podría volverse más común para reducir desperdicios y aumentar la fibra.

**Resumen en una frase** – Comer la piel y semillas de frutas y verduras aporta mucha más fibra, reduce el desperdicio y mejora la salud.
articles.image_prompt: A warm, detailed painting of a vibrant kitchen scene featuring colorful whole fruits and vegetables—kiwi with skin, butternut squash with seeds and peel, watermelon with rind—arranged on a rustic wooden table, with soft natural light highlighting their textured skins and seeds, symbolizing nourishment and the beauty of using every part of the plant.
